extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century coffeehouse readers interested in manners, theatre, and social commentary
extracted.subtask_short: periodical essays on manners and theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Short, magazine-style essays and miscellanies (The Spectator) offering social criticism, theatrical guidance, and moral observations for a general, educated readership. Mixes theatre criticism, etiquette, and anecdotal moral lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty enhances beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty loses its force, if not accompanied with modesty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A humble opinion of oneself gains universal applause because it is not expected; the vain lose approbation through too great a sense of deserving it. (Illustrated by the contest between Clidamira and Damia: equal merit, but the diffident wins.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting — speak naturally ("trippingly")
rubrics_metrics.description: "Speak the speech as I pronounce it to you, trippingly on the tongue; but if you mouth it... I had as lieve the town-crier had spoke my lines."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver lines smoothly and naturally; avoid mouthing or over-enunciating that makes speech artificial or declamatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting — avoid exaggerated gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nor do not saw the air too much with your hand thus; but use all gently."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gestures sparingly and gracefully rather than violent or mechanical arm-waving; gestures should support, not overwhelm, speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting — temperance in passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in "the torrent, tempest, and... the whirlwind of passion, you must acquire and beget a temperance that may give it smoothness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion should be controlled so it reads as natural and smooth rather than frantic; maintain a balance that preserves clarity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting — avoid overacting
rubrics_metrics.description: "It offends me to the soul, to see a robustious periwig-pated fellow tear a passion to tatters... I could have such a fellow whipped for overdoing termagant: it out-Herods Herod."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not tear a passion to rags or 'out-Herod Herod' — overdone acting may elicit cheap laughter from the unskilful but will grieve the judicious; overacting defeats the purpose of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting — suit action to the word and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: "Suit the action to the word, the word to the action; with this special observance, that you overstep not the modesty of nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure physical action and vocal delivery match the text's meaning and tone; preserve naturalness and avoid affectations that break credibility. The aim is to 'hold as it were the mirror up to Nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting — clowns/fools must not ad-lib to provoke laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let those that play your clowns, speak no more than is set down for them: for there be of them that will of themselves laugh, to set on some quantity of barren spectators to laugh too... that is villanous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors playing comic parts should not invent extra lines or antics to manufacture audience laughter at the expense of the play's integrity; such behaviour is petty ambition and harmful to the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate people by merit, not fortune or figure
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is my way to consider men as they stand in merit, and not according to their fortune or figure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess persons based on talents and character rather than wealth, status, or outward appearance; notice and praise genuine ability even in obscure stations (example: the barber Mr. Salter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive antiquarian claims in collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Collectors should not impose spurious names or false origins on objects (example: a common straw hat presented as 'Pontius Pilate's wife's chamber-maid's sister's hat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label and present curiosities honestly; the writer condemns using 'learning and antiquity' as a pretext to deceive the public and scandalize the well-disposed. Remove items that mislead or promote heterodox opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking snuff signals lack of reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: "Taking snuff... is done only to supply with sensations the want of reflection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The habit of taking snuff is satirically presented as a device to replace thought or conversation; borrowing snuff (having no box) is an even poorer sign — like schoolboys asking for 'a little sense.' The habit is widespread but marks intellectual emptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's writing: favour truth and simplicity over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding 'history written by a woman': 'it will not... be demanded, that style and ornament shall be so much consulted, as truth and simplicity; which latter qualities we may more justly pretend to beyond the other sex.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing on matters of love and domestic affairs (the announced remit), prioritize truthful, simple expression rather than elaborate stylistic flourish; modest aims and plainness are virtues in this genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cosmetics (circumspection) to look outward, not for self-admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Bickerstaff's 'Circumspection Water' "if you go to a glass, with design to admire your face, it immediately changes it into downright deformity. If you consult it only to look with a better countenance upon your friends, it immediately gives an alacrity to the visage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic prescription: cosmetics or devices intended to improve social appearance work when used to present oneself towards others (modest display), but self-admiration corrupts their effect. Timing and the subject's temperament (not in the rage of distemper; new brides or newly promoted should wait) affect efficacy; effects extend to others (can cure jealousy or detraction).
